Garlick
gär'lĭk
n. (a pungent bulb of the onion kind; last named in Israel's list of what Egypt gave them)
Old English garleac, from gar, a spear, and leac, a leek — the spear-leek, named for its pointed leaves. The Hebrew shum occurs only in Numbers 11:5.

Biblical Definition

It stands at the end of the list: “We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” (Num 11:5). Garlic was a staple of the Egyptian labourer — strong, cheap, and eaten with bread — and its appearing last gives the sentence its rhythm and its pathos. This is what the exodus was weighed against. The setting is a whole camp weeping in the doors of their tents, the mixt multitude falling a lusting and the children of Israel weeping with them, and the anger of the LORD kindled greatly; and the same chapter shows Moses at the end of himself, asking whether he had conceived all this people. Quails came, and with them a plague, and the place was named the graves of lust. Nothing in Scripture forbids garlic. What Numbers 11 records is an appetite that had grown loud enough to speak for the whole congregation, and a God who granted the request and sent leanness with it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines garlic as a plant of the genus Allium, having a bulbous root of a strong and offensive smell and a pungent taste, much used in cookery.

GARLIC, n. [Sax. garleac; gar, a dart, and leac, a leek.] A plant of the genus Allium.

The root is bulbous, of a strong and offensive smell, and an acrid pungent taste.

The leeks, and the onions, and the garlick. Num. xi.

GARLIC-EATER, n. A low fellow. [Not used.]

Key Scripture

Num 11:5 — "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:"

Num 11:6 — "But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes."

Php 3:19 — "Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)"

Pro 15:17 — "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith."

Modern Corruption

Appetite is treated as a fixed given to be satisfied rather than a servant to be governed, and Numbers 11 shows a whole nation moved by it.

expand to see more

Paul's phrase for a certain kind of man is blunt: whose God is their belly. He is writing about professing enemies of the cross, and the mark he gives is not gross debauchery but a life organised around appetite. Numbers 11 shows a nation in that condition for a season. They are not worshipping an idol; they are naming vegetables, and weeping. The camp's grievance is genuinely felt, widely shared, and completely unanswerable by argument, which is what makes appetite so powerful in a community: it does not have to make a case. Modern life is arranged to keep every appetite within a few minutes' reach and to present the satisfying of them as a duty to oneself, so that the very idea of denying an appetite reads as self-harm rather than as discipline. The fasting the church has almost entirely lost was the ordinary Christian answer.

The chapter's outcome deserves to be preached whole. God gave them what they asked. Quails came in from the sea, and they had flesh a whole month, and while it was yet between their teeth the wrath of God fell, and the place was named Kibrothhattaavah — the graves of lust. The psalmist summarises it in a line that ought to make any man careful what he insists on: he gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul. That is a real and terrible mercy withheld: not every denied prayer is a hard providence, and not every granted one is a kindness. Proverbs sets the whole matter at a table, where it belongs: better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shum (H7762), garlic, occurring only at Numbers 11:5; with taavah (H8378), craving, and razon (H7332), leanness, from the psalm's comment on the episode.

expand to see more

Hebrew shum (H7762) — garlic; the last item in Israel's remembered list; Numbers 11:5.

Hebrew betsel (H1211) — onion; named beside it in the same verse; Numbers 11:5.

Hebrew taavah (H8378) — desire, lust, craving; the name of the burial place, Kibrothhattaavah; Numbers 11:34.

Hebrew razon (H7332) — leanness, wasting; he sent leanness into their soul; Psalm 106:15.

Greek koilia (G2836) — the belly; whose God is their belly; Philippians 3:19.

Usage

"“The leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” — the exodus weighed against a market stall."

"“Whose God is their belly” — the New Testament's blunt name for the condition."

"“Better is a dinner of herbs where love is” — the same table, weighed differently."
